London, March 1727.

From the notebook of Isaac Newton, natural philosopher, Master of His Majesty's Mint and President of the Royal Society.

The weather this week has been fair, and I have been able to resume the work postponed since the autumn. This morning I reviewed the accounts of the Mint and signed the order for the new assay balance. There is a letter from Halley still to answer, and the sheets of the third edition are late from the printer. Yesterday I said to my assistant:

"Is there anything else?"

He answered:

"There is a young man here with some questions for you, sir. I think he is a gentleman."

I looked at the man, who was in his mid-twenties, tall, slender, his hair cut short, wearing a fine suit of grey cloth with a dark blue waistcoat. He was rather pale, his face pinched.

"We must get on with the work."

The accounts were in order, the balance will be a fine instrument, and I expect that the sheets will be delivered tomorrow. I can resume the work. I am ready to resume the work.

And yet, this evening, I find myself unable to do so. A headache, a pain in the chest. It is not the same as before. I do not think it is the same at all.

"Take this with you, and find the solution to the problem."

The young man's face paled. "It is not done?"

"I am not satisfied that it is done."

"But you have been working at it for three years, sir."

"And I have not succeeded in three years. This is a problem worthy of me; I shall solve it."

The young man bowed and departed.

'Why did you not watch?' I said, and I saw that the assistant was crying.
